title: Hidden fees in R&D tax credit advisor contracts
description: Hidden fees in U.S. R&D tax credit contracts include contingent fees, excluded audit defense, disbursements and refund-claim work.
summary: This page explains hidden fees in U.S. R&D tax credit advisor contracts, including contingent fees, excluded audit defense, disbursements and refund-claim work. Businesses should confirm how the fee is calculated and what it excludes, because a fee contingent on the credit can create a Form 8886 disclosure obligation, with § 6707A penalties for not filing.

body.text: This page explains hidden fees in U.S. R&D tax credit advisor contracts, including contingent fees, excluded audit defense, disbursements and refund-claim work. Businesses should confirm how the fee is calculated and what it excludes, because a fee contingent on the credit can create a Form 8886 disclosure obligation, with § 6707A penalties for not filing.
Analysis is labeled as analysis. This is general information, not legal or tax advice.
Executive Summary

Before signing an R&D tax credit engagement letter, a business should know three things: how the fee is calculated, which costs sit outside that fee (audit defense above all), and whether the fee structure itself creates a federal disclosure obligation. Failure to file Form 8886 for such a transaction carries a penalty under IRC § 6707A.

One further point bears directly on what a buyer is paying for. Because many research credits are claimed on amended returns, the IRS's refund-claim specificity requirements (Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F, as administered through a transition period now extended through January 10, 2027) determine whether the claim an advisor prepares is even processable. An engagement letter that does not say who produces that information, and whether curing a deficient claim is inside the fee, leaves a cost that can surface only after filing.
The Credit Being Protected

The fee in an engagement letter matters because it is paid out of a credit of limited size. Under IRC § 41(a)(1), the regular credit is 20 percent of qualified research expenses (QREs) above a base amount; the elective alternative simplified credit under § 41(c)(4) is 14 percent of QREs above 50 percent of the prior three-year average (6 percent where there were no QREs in any of those years).

QREs consist of in-house research expenses (wages for qualified services, supplies, and amounts paid for the right to use computers) and contract research expenses, generally counted at 65 percent of the amount paid (§ 41(b)).

The "substantially all" rule in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) treats all of an employee's wages as qualified when wages for qualified services are at least 80 percent of that employee's wages for the year.

Analysis: these mechanics matter to fee review because a percentage-of-credit fee is computed on the gross credit, while the business's real benefit may be smaller after the § 280C(c) reduction election, carryforward timing, or a later audit adjustment. A buyer comparing proposals should ask whether the fee base is the credit claimed, the credit actually used against tax, or the credit sustained after examination.

Costs Outside the Quoted Fee
Audit defense

Its cited source, a pricing guide published by Acena Consulting ("How Much Does An R&D Study Cost?", undated), calls audit defense usually the largest add-on and estimates that such add-ons can raise cost by 15% to 100%. It also notes that some firms bundle "free" audit defense into a higher fee, and others bill hourly with a cap of around 30% of credits. These are one firm's estimates without independent data.
Correction. That page describes DCAA audits of government contractors' costs. It is not an IRS examination of a research credit claim, and FAR compliance checks are not part of an R&D credit audit.
Disbursements, software, travel and review charges

The same Acena guide lists travel at $500 to $5,000 when work is onsite, documentation software from about $50 per user per month to $5,000 or more, and optional quarterly reviews at $1,000 to $3,000 per quarter. These are verified as that publisher's estimates only.
Refund assignment and agency agreements

Its source, Cost Care Tax, addresses the UK and HMRC (including the Form 64-8 agent authority). Its points on loss of oversight, refunds diverted before the business sees them, assignments left in place for later refunds, and accountants losing visibility are accurately summarized. Correction of scope: they describe UK practice.
Scope of work

The Journal of Accountancy (November 1, 2025) describes the engagement letter as the record of services, responsibilities and expectations, and criticizes letters that do not define scope or deliverables. It also notes that a defined scope lets the firm identify and bill additional work, which is the mechanism by which an unclear scope turns into extra fees.

Added in-scope point. For research credits claimed on amended returns, scope now has a regulatory dimension. Under the IRS's refund-claim requirements described below, a claim that lacks the required business-component and expense information can be rejected in full unless it is perfected within 45 days of an IRS deficiency letter during the transition period. Beginning with tax years starting in 2026, most original-return filers must also complete Section G of Form 6765 (business-component detail); the IRS made Section G optional for tax year 2025 in IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025). Analysis: whether preparing Section G detail, answering a deficiency letter, and re-filing a perfected claim fall inside the quoted fee is a scope question the engagement letter should answer expressly, because these are the tasks most likely to be billed later as "additional work."

body.text: Contingent Fees and Reportable Transactions
The contractual protection test

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.6011-4(b)(4)(i), a transaction has contractual protection if the taxpayer or a related party may get a full or partial refund of fees when the intended tax consequences are not sustained, or if fees are contingent on realizing the tax benefits. Under (b)(4)(ii), only fees paid to a person who makes a statement about the potential tax consequences count. Under (b)(4)(iii)(B), refundable or contingent fees are disregarded where the advisor's statement is given only after the taxpayer has entered into the transaction and reported its consequences on a filed return, and the advisor has not previously received fees for it.

Rev. Proc. 2007-20 (effective January 26, 2007) lists credits whose contingent or refundable fees are disregarded: the work opportunity credit (§ 51), welfare-to-work (§ 51A), Indian employment (§ 45A(a)), low-income housing (§ 42(a)), new markets (§ 45D(a)), empowerment zone employment (§ 1396(a)), renewal community employment (§ 1400H) and the employee retention credit under § 1400R. The research credit under § 41 is not on the list. CohnReznick (February 27, 2025) draws the same conclusion.

Analysis: whether a particular engagement is reportable turns on the facts, including when the advisor's statement was given and whether the post-filing exception in (b)(4)(iii)(B) applies. A taxpayer facing the question should have it reviewed before filing.
Disclosure and the § 6707A penalty

Participants in a reportable transaction disclose it on Form 8886, Reportable Transaction Disclosure Statement (current form revision December 2019; instructions revised October 2022). Correction: Form 8886 is the taxpayer's disclosure; material advisors file their own disclosure on Form 8918, as CohnReznick notes.
Under IRC § 6707A(b), the penalty is 75 percent of the decrease in tax resulting from the transaction, subject to these limits:
Correction of emphasis: A contractual protection transaction that is not also listed is capped at $50,000 for an entity and $10,000 for an individual, per failure.

Circular 230 and its limits

Circular 230 § 10.27(b) (31 CFR 10.27, applicable to fee arrangements entered into after March 26, 2008) bars practitioners from charging contingent fees for services in connection with any matter before the IRS, except for an IRS examination or challenge to a return (including an amended return or refund claim filed within 120 days of written notice of the exam), claims solely for statutory interest or penalties, and judicial proceedings.

In Ridgely v. Lew, No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC) (D.D.C. July 16, 2014), reported at 55 F. Supp. 3d 89, the court held that the IRS lacked statutory authority to enforce § 10.27's contingent-fee restrictions for preparing and filing ordinary refund claims before any examination begins, and permanently enjoined enforcement (memorandum opinion). The IRS did not appeal (Accounting Today). Many R&D credits are claimed on amended returns or refund claims, so a licensed practitioner charging a contingent fee for an ordinary refund claim is not, for that reason alone, violating an enforceable rule. The reportable-transaction rules are separate and still apply.

Pending change (added). On December 20, 2024, Treasury and the IRS released proposed regulations (REG-116610-20, published in the Federal Register December 26, 2024) to update Circular 230. In response to Ridgely, the proposal would remove § 10.27 entirely, withdraw the 2009 proposed contingent-fee regulations, and instead treat charging a contingent fee for preparing an original return, an amended return, or a claim for refund or credit as "disreputable conduct" subject to sanction. The proposed definition of a contingent fee covers fees based on a percentage of the refund or tax saved, fees dependent on a specific tax outcome, and arrangements that reimburse the fee if a position is not sustained. A public hearing was held March 6, 2025, and more than 150 comments were submitted (The CPA Journal; NYSSCPA). This review found no final regulation adopting these changes; as proposed, they would take effect 30 days after final regulations are published. Analysis: if finalized as proposed, a percentage-of-credit fee for preparing an amended-return R&D claim by a Circular 230 practitioner would again be sanctionable, which makes the fee basis a term buyers should expect to see renegotiated in multi-year engagements.
Section 174 and Fee Budgeting

Correction (law changed): the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, § 70302) added IRC § 174A, which restores immediate deduction of domestic research or experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, with an election to amortize over at least 60 months. Foreign research costs remain subject to 15-year amortization under amended § 174. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 (released August 28, 2025; Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-38) sets out the elections, including an election for eligible small businesses (non-tax-shelter taxpayers meeting the § 448(c) gross receipts test, average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less, for the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024) to apply § 174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, and an election for all taxpayers to deduct remaining unamortized 2022 to 2024 domestic costs over one or two years (Crowe; BDO; Eide Bailly).
Analysis: Buyers should confirm whether that work is inside an R&D credit engagement's quoted fee or billed separately.
Audit Exposure Behind the Fee Question
Its source, Tax Point Advisors, attributes a 10% claim rate to "the IRS" without a citation, so the figure is unverified.

The Tax Adviser (April 2022) reports that the IRS's 2008 Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide noted a growing trend of taxpayers and representatives submitting prepackaged material. The same article describes Field Attorney Advice 20214101F (October 2021), which requires specific information for research credit refund claims. K-38 Consulting, an advisory firm, states that expense calculation errors cause the most financial damage in R&D credit audits; this is a firm's view, not an IRS statistic.

Correction and update (refund-claim requirements). Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F identified five items a valid research credit refund claim must include: the business components that form the factual basis of the claim; for each business component, the research activities performed; the individuals who performed each activity; the information each individual sought to discover; and total qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be shown on Form 6765). The IRS's January 2022 FAQs and LB&I interim guidance did not apply the rule immediately and without recourse; they set a grace period through January 10, 2022, and then a transition period in which a timely but deficient claim receives a letter (Letter 6428 or 6426C) and 45 days to be perfected. Only if the missing information is not supplied within that window is the entire claim rejected (IRS; EY). The transition period has been extended repeatedly, most recently in IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), through January 10, 2027 (BDO; Grant Thornton). For refund claims postmarked after June 18, 2024, the IRS's updated guidance requires the claim to identify all business components and their research activities, together with total QREs by category.

Form 6765 itself has been revised. The IRS made the new Section G (business-component reporting) optional for all filers for tax year 2025 and has announced it will be mandatory for most filers beginning with tax year 2026, with exceptions that include qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax offset and taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less (Cherry Bekaert). The updated Form 6765 instructions (Rev. December 2025) no longer cite Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F by number; practitioner commentary advises continuing to follow its requirements for refund claims for years before Section G becomes mandatory (KPMG). Analysis: these requirements tie directly to hidden-fee risk. An advisor whose contingent or fixed fee is earned on filing, but whose engagement excludes responding to a deficiency letter, leaves the client to pay separately for the work that keeps the claim alive.
Contract Checklist
Analysis, drawn from the verified material above:

items: Is any part of the fee calculated on, or refundable based on, the credit realized or sustained? If so, consider the reportable-transaction rules in Treas. Reg. § 1.6011-4(b)(4) before filing.
Is audit defense included, and does that cover only the advisor's time or also outside CPAs and attorneys, appeals and litigation?
Are travel, software, quarterly reviews and other disbursements included, capped, or excluded in writing?
Does the letter define deliverables and the documentation the advisor will produce, including what is needed for a refund claim to meet the IRS specificity requirements?

If the claim is on an amended return, is responding to an IRS deficiency letter within the 45-day perfection window part of the quoted fee? For tax years beginning in 2026 and later, is preparation of Form 6765 Section G business-component detail included?

If the advisor is a Circular 230 practitioner and the fee is contingent, does the letter address what happens to the fee basis if the proposed Circular 230 amendments are finalized during the engagement?
Do refunds go to the business's own account, with its accountant able to review the claim?
